theory.intro: $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ says $X$ is normal with mean $\mu$ and **variance** $\sigma^{2}$, the square of the standard deviation. The **standard normal distribution** is $Z\sim N(0,1)$, the one curve with mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$.
facts: In $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ the second number is the variance, so the standard deviation is its square root.
$X\sim N(70,25)$ and $X\sim N(70,5^{2})$ describe the same variable, with mean $70$ and standard deviation $5$.
A distribution is standard normal only when both $\mu=0$ and $\sigma=1$; any other pair is non-standard.
Standardising uses $Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$, which subtracts the mean and then divides by the standard deviation.
Every normal variable standardises to the same curve, so one table of $z$ values serves all of them.
A $z$ value counts standard deviations, so it has no units even when $X$ is measured in grams or hours.
The score $x=\mu+\sigma$ always maps to $z=1$, whatever the mean and standard deviation happen to be.
steps: Read the first number in $N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ as the mean
Read the second number as the variance $\sigma^{2}$
Take the square root of the variance to get the standard deviation

workedExamples.question_text:
$X\sim N(-8,36)$ and $Y\sim N(18,0.7^{2})$.
State the mean and standard deviation of each variable. Is either distribution standard normal?
workedExamples.solution_text:
For $X$:
$\begin{align*}\mu_X&=-8\\\sigma_X^{2}&=36\\\sigma_X&=\sqrt{36}\\&=6\end{align*}$
For $Y$:
$\begin{align*}\mu_Y&=18\\\sigma_Y^{2}&=0.7^{2}\\\sigma_Y&=0.7\end{align*}$
Neither is standard normal. A standard normal distribution has mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$.

workedExamples.question_text:
$X\sim N(84,64)$.
Find the z-score for $x=72$ and interpret it.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\sigma&=\sqrt{64}\\&=8\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\&=\frac{72-84}{8}\\&=-1.5\end{align*}$
The score is $1.5$ standard deviations below the mean.

$X\sim N(4.2,2.25)$.
State the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.

$X\sim N(60,16)$ and $Y\sim N(500,100)$.
Show that $P(X<68)$ and $P(Y<520)$ are equal.
development.solution_text:
For $X$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{16}=4$.
$z$
$=\frac{68-60}{4}$
$=2$
For $Y$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{100}=10$.
$z$
$=\frac{520-500}{10}$
$=2$
Both scores standardise to $z=2$, so both probabilities equal $P(Z<2)$.

mastery.question_text:
$X\sim N(\mu,6^{2})$.
The score $x=43$ standardises to $z=1.5$.
Find $\mu$.

$X\sim N(160,\sigma^{2})$, and the score $x=172$ standardises to $z=0.8$.
Find $\sigma$.

$X\sim N(25,9)$ and $Y\sim N(25,36)$.
A score of $31$ is recorded on each scale.
Explain which score is the more extreme.
mastery.solution_text:
For $X$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{9}=3$.
$z$
$=\frac{31-25}{3}$
$=2$
For $Y$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{36}=6$.
$z$
$=\frac{31-25}{6}$
$=1$
Both scores map onto the same standard normal curve, and $31$ sits two standard deviations out on the $X$ scale but only one on the $Y$ scale.
The score of $31$ on the $X$ scale is the more extreme.
